# A Political Crisis, Not a Fiscal One: France's Floating Debt Crisis, 1924-1926

As French yields hit a 24-year high, a century-old precedent: between 1924 and 1926 France did not run out of money, it ran out of credibility. Archival evidence from the Banque de France and the Bank of England shows how contemporaries diagnosed the crisis, and why Poincaré's return turned the market before any reform was passed.

Grégoire Peverelli, Xiao Li, Alexandru Degeratu, Francisco Valente Daniel, Jaume Monclús i Bori and Franklin Xiong25 October 202624 min read

## Why this matters now

In October 2026, France's 10-year borrowing cost briefly rose above 5% for the first time since July 2002, and the gap over German Bunds widened past 150 basis points, the widest since the euro area debt crisis of 2011. A 2027 budget meant to cut the deficit from 5.4% to 5% of GDP has no majority in a divided National Assembly, the streets have seen more than a month of protests, and the Agence France Trésor plans a record €340 billion of borrowing next year to fund the deficit and refinance maturing debt. This week Moody's held France at Aa3 with a negative outlook, pointing less to the arithmetic than to the fragmentation of French politics.

A century ago, France lived through a crisis with a strikingly similar shape. Between 1924 and 1926 the French state did not run out of money; it ran out of credibility. Governments fell one after another, investors stopped renewing short-term Treasury paper, and the franc collapsed. Then a single change at the top, Raymond Poincaré's return in July 1926, turned the market before any reform was passed.

The differences matter. Public debt then exceeded 200% of national income; today it is around 119% of GDP. Modern France borrows mostly long, in euros, with the European Central Bank in the background, while the Third Republic depended on a rolling stock of short-dated bills and a central bank that was quietly running out of room. Yet the core lesson of the paper below is the one markets are pricing again: sovereign debt sustainability depends as much on political credibility as on fiscal capacity. We republish our research here, lightly edited, as a historical reference point for the present.

---

A Political Crisis, Not a Fiscal One: Contemporary Diagnoses of the French Floating Debt Problem, 1924-1926

## Abstract

Between 1924 and 1926, France teetered on the edge of sovereign default not because it was fiscally insolvent, but because it could not roll over its debt. Drawing on archival evidence from the Banque de France and Bank of England, this paper reconstructs how policymakers at the time understood the crisis. Both sources converge on the same diagnosis: the collapse of France's floating debt market was a political credibility problem, not a fiscal one. Fragmented governments could not commit; without credibility, even a technically sound refinancing system unravelled. The proof is Poincaré's stabilisation in July 1926: markets recovered before a single reform was enacted. The French case offers a timeless lesson: sovereign debt sustainability depends as much on political credibility as on fiscal capacity.

## 1. Introduction

Between 1924 and 1926, France teetered on the edge of sovereign default not because it was fiscally insolvent, but because it could not roll over its debt. Drawing on archival evidence from the Banque de France and Bank of England, this paper reconstructs how policymakers at the time understood the crisis. Both sources converge on the same diagnosis: the collapse of France's floating debt market was a political credibility problem, not a fiscal one. Fragmented governments could not commit; without credibility, even a technically sound refinancing system unravelled. The proof is Poincaré's stabilisation: markets recovered before a single reform was enacted. Section 2 provides historical context. Section 3 reviews the literature. Section 4 outlines the sources and methodological approach. Section 5 presents the archival evidence. Section 6 discusses the findings. Section 7 concludes.

## 2. Historical context

Leonetto Cappiello, "Emprunt National 1920", poster for the Banque Nationale de Crédit, printed by Devambez, Paris, 1920.

### The post-war debt burden

The fiscal legacy of World War I left the French state structurally fragile. To finance extraordinary reconstruction costs, the government relied heavily on Bons de la Défense Nationale (BDNs), short-term treasury bills requiring continuous rollover. By 1924-1926, the inability to refinance maturing obligations threatened a complete collapse of French public credit.

By July 1920, public debt had risen from roughly 30 billion francs in 1914 to over 200 billion francs (Jèze, 1921, p. 191; Figure 1). A significant external component was owed primarily to Britain and the United States in foreign currencies, which, in contrast to BDNs, could not be inflated away (Jèze, 1921, p. 191).

Figure 1. Composition of French public debt, 1920 (millions of francs). Source: Jèze (1921, p. 191).

### The reparations illusion

French war finance rested on a single assumption: that German reparations would cover the costs. When that proved false, the government faced an enormous debt overhang and no credible plan to service it (Figure 2; End, 2019, pp. 125-132).

BDNs had reached 44.2 billion francs outstanding by July 1920 (Jèze, 1921, p. 190). Their appeal rested on simplicity and favourable tax treatment. However, their coupons were administratively fixed and adjusted only twice between 1919 and 1926, leaving the Treasury with no market-based tool to retain investors when confidence weakened (Makinen & Woodward, 1989, pp. 193, 205).

The François-Marsal Convention of 1920, under which the Treasury committed to repay two billion francs annually to the Bank of France, was intended as a signal of monetary orthodoxy aiming to address fiscal dominance (Prati, 1991, p. 216; Bordo et al., 2007, p. 12). As conditions deteriorated, the government's failure to honour these repayments became a visible marker of fiscal distress (Makinen & Woodward, 1989, p. 194).

Figure 2. French fiscal balance, 1919-1929. Authors' elaboration based on Jordà, Schularick & Taylor (2017). Values in new francs (1 new franc = 100 old francs).

### The floating debt problem

By the early 1920s, France faced what authorities described as a "floating debt problem" (François-Marsal, 1927, p. 197). BDNs had maturities of up to one year and required continuous rollover; between 1921 and 1926 the stock of Treasury paper outstanding fluctuated between roughly 46 and 67 billion francs (Prati, 1991, Fig. 2; Makinen & Woodward, 1989, Table II).

The fragility was structural: falling demand pushed yields up, raising servicing costs and eroding confidence further. François-Marsal warned that once doubts arose, the "circuit of currency" would break down, bondholders would demand repayment "en masse", and the floating debt would become "the most terrible of all problems" (François-Marsal, 1927, pp. 196-198). Stabilisation was not undesirable; it was simply politically and fiscally unattainable (François-Marsal, 1927, p. 189; Bordo et al., 2003).

### The erosion of confidence, 1922-1924

Confidence began deteriorating in mid-1922 following the failure of the Genoa Conference. France's refusal to reschedule German reparations triggered sustained franc depreciation. "Speculators anticipated that a rise in Bank of France notes in circulation would lead to depreciation, and they acted accordingly" (Eichengreen, 1982, p. 75). Subscriptions to Treasury paper peaked in late 1922 and entered a prolonged decline (Prati, 1991, pp. 216-217).

The occupation of the Ruhr in January 1923 was a last attempt to enforce reparations by force. Its failure was decisive. Bond prices collapsed in late 1923; a medium-term issue failed outright in January 1924, and the franc lost nearly half its dollar value within five months (Makinen & Woodward, 1989, p. 202; Eichengreen, 1982, p. 71).

Figure 3. Yields on French sovereign bonds traded in London, 1919-1929. Authors' elaboration based on the Investor's Monthly Manual. The chart reflects international bond yields, not the domestic BDN market.

Under Poincaré's second government, France secured a 20% increase in indirect taxes and used this to obtain an international loan from Morgan and Lazard Frères (Makinen & Woodward, 1989, p. 195). The loan sharply (but temporarily) stabilised confidence, briefly pulling yields back from a peak of 21 per cent (Figure 3). Nevertheless, note circulation continued to rise, and government borrowing from the central bank approached the statutory ceiling of 41 billion francs (Prati, 1991, p. 218; Figure 4).

Figure 4. Money supply in France, 1920-1930. Authors' elaboration based on Jordà, Schularick & Taylor (2017). M1 = note circulation + sight deposits. Values in new francs.

### The political dimension

The 1924 elections brought the Cartel des Gauches to power. Its proposals for capital levies and forced debt consolidation alarmed bondholders with the threat of partial repudiation (Figure 5). However, these programmes were politically impractical (Bordo et al., 2007, p. 10).

Figure 5. French government bill rate (short-term debt), 1922-1932. Authors' elaboration based on Jordà, Schularick & Taylor (2017).

Rollover difficulties intensified throughout 1925, and matters worsened sharply when it was revealed that the Bank of France had hidden the true extent of its advances to the state. Confidence collapsed: investors refused to renew short-term debt and the franc depreciated rapidly (Figure 7). France was on the verge of runaway inflation (Figure 6; Makinen & Woodward, 1989, p. 195; Prati, 1991, pp. 213, 220).

Figure 6. French inflation rate, 1919-1929. Authors' elaboration based on Jordà, Schularick & Taylor (2017).

### The rollover crisis of 1925-1926

The crisis peaked in mid-1925 when unusually large volumes of short-term debt matured simultaneously (Prati, 1991, p. 221). Unable to roll them over, the government repeatedly raised statutory limits on note issuance and central bank lending (Figure 4). The scale of dependence was captured by a French economist writing in April 1925:

> "It is common knowledge that the French Treasury is fed daily by the sale of National Defence Bonds of three, six, or twelve months maturity. The total amount of these bonds in circulation is about 56 milliards, and they are continually renewed. I have heard this renewal described by a financial specialist as a miracle." (The Economist, 11 April 1925, p. 710)

Between April 1925 and July 1926, France saw twelve finance ministers and seven governments, none of whom secured durable support for reform (Prati, 1991, Table 2; End, 2019, p. 125). By May-July 1926 wholesale prices were rising at annualised rates approaching 300 per cent, the franc was in freefall (Figure 7), and monetary financing had become unavoidable (Makinen & Woodward, 1989, p. 195; Eichengreen, 1982, pp. 75-76; Prati, 1991, pp. 221-222).

Figure 7. French franc exchange rate (francs per US dollar), 1919-1929. Authors' elaboration based on Federal Reserve Board, Banking and Monetary Statistics.

### The Poincaré stabilisation

Poincaré's expected return to power in July 1926 restored confidence almost immediately. His reputation for fiscal prudence stabilised the franc within weeks (Eichengreen, 1982, p. 76; François-Marsal, 1927, p. 198). His programme centred on the creation of a dedicated sinking fund, the Caisse Autonome d'Amortissement, which was financed through earmarked taxes to guarantee debt service (Makinen & Woodwar
